solution: The line \(x+y=0\) has slope \(-1\) (inclination \(135^\circ\)). A required line through the origin makes angle \(\alpha\) with it, so its slope is \(m=\tan(135^\circ\pm\alpha)\). Then \(m\) satisfies (with \(m=y/x\)) a quadratic whose sum and product give the pair. Sum of slopes \(=\tan(135+\alpha)+\tan(135-\alpha)\) and product \(=\tan(135+\alpha)\tan(135-\alpha)\). Using \(\tan(135^\circ+\alpha)=\dfrac{-1+\tan\alpha}{1+\tan\alpha}\) and \(\tan(135^\circ-\alpha)=\dfrac{-1-\tan\alpha}{1-\tan\alpha}\): the product is \(\dfrac{(-1+\tan\alpha)(-1-\tan\alpha)}{(1+\tan\alpha)(1-\tan\alpha)}=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=1\), and the sum is \(\dfrac{-(1-\tan\alpha)^2-(1+\tan\alpha)^2}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=\dfrac{-2(1+\tan^2\alpha)}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=-2\sec2\alpha\). Thus the pair is \(y^2-(\text{sum})xy+(\text{product})x^2=0\Rightarrow y^2+2\sec2\alpha\,xy+x^2=0\), i.e. \(x^2+2(\sec2\alpha)xy+y^2=0\). Hence proved.
note: the sum-of-slopes step broke off ('... computing gives'); it is -2(1 + tan²α)/(1 - tan²α) = -2 sec 2α, and the product's denominator is (1 + tan α)(1 - tan α).
